front: Oxente, e quem foi que disse isso?
pronunciation: oh-SHEHN-chee, ee KENG FOY keh JEE-see EE-soo?
back: What on earth? And who said that?
context: 'Oxente' (or 'oxe') expresses surprise, disbelief or annoyance. It is the most iconic Northeastern interjection.

front: Vixe, esqueci a carteira em casa!
pronunciation: VEE-shee, ehs-keh-SEE ah kahr-TAY-rah eng KAH-zah!
back: Oh no, I left my wallet at home!
context: 'Vixe' (from 'Virgem Maria!') signals surprise or alarm. Now used all over Brazil.

front: Eita, que esse forró tá bom demais!
pronunciation: AY-tah, keh EH-see foh-RROH TAH BOHNG jee-MAHYS!
back: Wow, this forró is really good!
context: 'Eita' = wow / whoa. Forró is the Northeast's signature dance music, especially during the June festivals.

front: Aquele show foi arretado!
pronunciation: ah-KEH-lee SHOH FOY ah-rreh-TAH-doo!
back: That show was amazing!
context: 'Arretado' = amazing, excellent. It can also mean angry ('ficou arretado' = he got mad); context decides.

front: Massa, a gente se vê no fim de semana então.
pronunciation: MAH-sah, ah ZHEHN-chee see VEH noo FEENG jee seh-MAH-nah ehn-TOWNG.
back: Cool, see you at the weekend then.
context: 'Massa' = cool, great, very common in Pernambuco and Ceará.

front: Tô com fome, visse? Bora comer alguma coisa.
pronunciation: TOH kohng FOH-mee, VEE-see? BOH-rah koh-MEHR ahl-GOO-mah KOY-zah.
back: I'm hungry, you know? Let's go eat something.
context: 'Visse?' (from 'viu?') is a tag question typical of Recife and Pernambuco, like 'right?' or 'you know?'.

front: Mainha mandou dizer que o almoço tá pronto.
pronunciation: mah-EE-nyah mahn-DOH jee-ZEHR keh oo ahl-MOH-soo TAH PROHN-too.
back: Mom says lunch is ready.
context: 'Mainha' and 'painho' (mommy, daddy) are typical of Bahia and used by adults too.

front: Calma, meu rei, que tudo se resolve.
pronunciation: KAHL-mah, MEH-oo RRAY, keh TOO-doo see rreh-ZOHL-vee.
back: Easy, my friend, everything will work out.
context: 'Meu rei' (my king) and 'minha rainha' are affectionate forms of address typical of Salvador.

front: Colé de mermo, véi? Tudo tranquilo?
pronunciation: koh-LEH jee MEHR-moo, VEH-ee? TOO-doo trahn-KWEE-loo?
back: What's up, man? All good?
context: Salvador street greeting: 'Qual é de mesmo, velho?' contracted. 'Véi' (velho) = dude.

front: Esse trânsito tá barril hoje.
pronunciation: EH-see TRAHN-zee-too TAH bah-RREE-oo OH-zhee.
back: The traffic is crazy today.
context: In Bahia, 'barril' (barrel) describes a tense, difficult or chaotic situation. 'Tá barril' = things are rough.

front: Vai sair com essa chuva? Lá ele!
pronunciation: VAHY sah-EER kohng EH-sah SHOO-vah? LAH EH-lee!
back: You're going out in this rain? Not me!
context: Bahian expression to distance yourself from something bad: 'God forbid it happens to me'.

front: Não fique avexado, que ainda dá tempo.
pronunciation: NOWNG FEE-kee ah-veh-SHAH-doo, keh ah-EEN-dah DAH TEHM-poo.
back: Don't rush, there's still time.
context: 'Avexado' = in a hurry, anxious. 'Avexar-se' = to rush.

front: Ela anda muito aperreada com as contas.
pronunciation: EH-lah AHN-dah MOOY-too ah-peh-rreh-AH-dah kohng ahs KOHN-tahs.
back: She's been really stressed about the bills.
context: 'Aperreado' = worried, troubled. 'Aperreio' = trouble, distress.

front: Aquele vaqueiro é um cabra da peste.
pronunciation: ah-KEH-lee vah-KAY-roo EH oong KAH-brah dah PEHS-chee.
back: That cowboy is one tough guy.
context: 'Cabra da peste' = a brave, tough person, a compliment from the sertão. 'Cabra' alone = guy.

front: Deixe de ser abestado, macho!
pronunciation: DAY-shee jee SEHR ah-behs-TAH-doo, MAH-shoo!
back: Stop being silly, man!
context: From Ceará: 'abestado' = silly, foolish; 'macho' = dude/man (used for anyone, even women, in Fortaleza).

front: A festa de ontem foi pai d'égua!
pronunciation: ah FEHS-tah jee ohn-TENG FOY PAHY DEH-gwah!
back: Yesterday's party was awesome!
context: 'Pai d'égua' (literally 'mare's father') = excellent, awesome. Typical of Ceará and Pará.

front: Pega o beco, que eu tô ocupado!
pronunciation: PEH-gah oo BEH-koo, keh EH-oo TOH oh-koo-PAH-doo!
back: Get lost, I'm busy!
context: 'Pegar o beco' (take the alley) = to leave, go away. Can be rude or playful depending on tone.

front: Rebola no mato esse papel aí.
pronunciation: rreh-BOH-lah noo MAH-too EH-see pah-PEH-oo ah-EE.
back: Throw that piece of paper away.
context: In Pernambuco and Ceará, 'rebolar no mato' (throw into the bush) = to throw away.

front: Para de mangar de mim!
pronunciation: PAH-rah jee mahn-GAHR jee MEENG!
back: Stop making fun of me!
context: 'Mangar de' = to mock, tease. Used across the Northeast.

front: Esse celular é fuleiro, quebrou na primeira semana.
pronunciation: EH-see seh-loo-LAHR EH foo-LAY-roo, keh-BROH nah pree-MAY-rah seh-MAH-nah.
back: This phone is junk; it broke in the first week.
context: 'Fuleiro' = shoddy, low quality. Also used for unreliable people.

front: Deixa de ser pirangueiro e paga a sua parte.
pronunciation: DAY-shah jee SEHR pee-rahn-GAY-roo ee PAH-gah ah SOO-ah PAHR-chee.
back: Stop being stingy and pay your share.
context: 'Pirangueiro' = cheapskate (Recife and Pernambuco). Elsewhere: 'pão-duro', 'mão de vaca'.

front: Que fuxico é esse sobre o casamento da vizinha?
pronunciation: keh foo-SHEE-koo EH EH-see SOH-bree oo kah-zah-MEHN-too dah vee-ZEE-nyah?
back: What's this gossip about the neighbor's wedding?
context: 'Fuxico' = gossip. 'Fuxiqueiro' = gossipy person. Common across the Northeast.

front: Ele ficou com a gota quando viu a conta.
pronunciation: EH-lee fee-KOH kohng ah GOH-tah KWAHN-doo VEE-oo ah KOHN-tah.
back: He went ballistic when he saw the bill.
context: 'Estar/ficar com a gota' = to be furious or out of control. 'É bom que só a gota' = it's extremely good.

front: Comi cuscuz com ovo e macaxeira no café da manhã.
pronunciation: koh-MEE koos-KOOS kohng OH-voo ee mah-kah-SHAY-rah noo kah-FEH dah mah-NYAH.
back: I had couscous with egg and cassava for breakfast.
context: Northeastern breakfast staples. 'Macaxeira' = cassava (called 'mandioca' or 'aipim' elsewhere).

front: Hoje tem doce de jerimum na casa da vó.
pronunciation: OH-zhee teng DOH-see jee zheh-ree-MOONG nah KAH-zah dah VOH.
back: Today there's pumpkin sweet at Grandma's.
context: 'Jerimum' = pumpkin in the Northeast ('abóbora' elsewhere). Many words come from Tupi.

front: O São João de Campina Grande é o maior do mundo, dizem.
pronunciation: oo SOWNG zhoh-OWNG jee kahm-PEE-nah GRAHN-jee EH oo mah-YOHR doo MOON-doo, JEE-zeng.
back: Campina Grande's São João festival is the biggest in the world, they say.
context: June festivals are the Northeast's biggest celebration; Campina Grande (Paraíba) and Caruaru (Pernambuco) compete for the title.

front: Bichinho, tá com frio? Vem pra cá.
pronunciation: bee-SHEE-nyoo, TAH kohng FREE-oo? VENG prah KAH.
back: Poor thing, are you cold? Come over here.
context: 'Bichinho' (little critter) is an affectionate or pitying form of address, very common in the Northeast.

front: Rapaz, você não sabe o que aconteceu!
pronunciation: rrah-PAHS, voh-SEH NOWNG SAH-bee oo keh ah-kohn-teh-SEH-oo!
back: Man, you won't believe what happened!
context: 'Rapaz' as an interjection to start a story, used even when talking to women.

front: Arrumei um emprego novo em Fortaleza.
pronunciation: ah-rroo-MAY oong ehm-PREH-goo NOH-voo eng fohr-tah-LEH-zah.
back: I got a new job in Fortaleza.
context: In the Northeast (and much of Brazil), 'arrumar' = to get, find (not just 'to tidy up').

front: Num precisa botar boneco por causa disso.
pronunciation: NOONG preh-SEE-zah boh-TAHR boh-NEH-koo pohr KOW-zah JEE-soo.
back: There's no need to make a fuss about it.
context: 'Botar boneco' = to make a scene or fuss (Pernambuco and Paraíba).

front: Esse menino é muito danado, não para quieto um minuto.
pronunciation: EH-see meh-NEE-noo EH MOOY-too dah-NAH-doo, NOWNG PAH-rah kee-EH-too oong mee-NOO-too.
back: This boy is a little rascal; he won't sit still for a minute.
context: 'Danado' = mischievous, naughty, but also clever or skilled ('danado de bom' = really good).

front: Diabéisso? Quem botou sal no café?
pronunciation: jee-ah-BAY-soo? KENG boh-TOH SOW noo kah-FEH?
back: What the heck is this? Who put salt in the coffee?
context: 'Diabéisso' = 'Que diabo é isso?' contracted into one word. Humorous and very Northeastern.

front: Tô morto de cansado, vou me deitar cedo.
pronunciation: TOH MOHR-too jee kahn-SAH-doo, VOH mee day-TAHR SEH-doo.
back: I'm dead tired; I'm going to bed early.
context: 'Morto de' + adjective = extremely. Common throughout Brazil and very frequent in the Northeast.

front: O sotaque nordestino abre as vogais: 'Recife' soa como 'Rècife'.
pronunciation: oo soh-TAH-kee nohr-dehs-CHEE-noo AH-bree ahz voh-GAHYS: rreh-SEE-fee SOH-ah KOH-moo rreh-SEE-fee.
back: The Northeastern accent opens the vowels: 'Recife' sounds like 'Rè-cife'.
context: Pretonic vowels are open in much of the Northeast ('pèrnambucano', 'rècife'). Many also keep 't' and 'd' hard before 'i': 'tia', 'dia'.

front: Cada lugar do Nordeste tem seu jeito de falar, não é tudo igual não.
pronunciation: KAH-dah loo-GAHR doo nohr-DEHS-chee teng SEH-oo ZHAY-too jee fah-LAHR, NOWNG EH TOO-doo ee-GWAHL NOWNG.
back: Every part of the Northeast has its own way of speaking; it's not all the same.
context: The Northeast has nine states with very different accents. Treating them as one is a common stereotype.
